PLOS Computational Biology.title: Ionic condition-dependent allostery shapes ribosomal dynamics
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Danis Yangaliev, Gürol M. Süel, S. Banu Ozkan Ionic composition is a key determinant of ribosomal RNA structure and function. Metal cations such as potassium (K+) and magnesium (Mg2+) stabilize rRNA architecture. While certain positions in the ribosome are strictly occupied by either potassium or magnesium for distinct structural or functional reasons, their broader role in modulating ribosomal dynamics remains poorly understood. Here, we use microsecond-scale coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations of the bacterial 70S ribosome to examine how ionic composition affects structural flexibility and long-range communication. We compare a native ribosome with experimentally resolved ions to two variants: a magnesium-enriched model, in which K+ ions are replaced with Mg2+, and a hydrated magnesium model. While these substitutions do not aim to reproduce physiological ionic conditions, they provide a controlled framework to isolate the physical effects of ion identity on ribosomal dynamics. Increasing magnesium content reduces ionic and backbone mobility and enhances rigidity within the ribosomal core. Dynamic Flexibility Index analysis shows that these changes extend beyond local coordination sites, producing flexibility shifts at distances exceeding 30 Å. Dynamic Coupling Index analysis further reveals that ionic perturbations reshape long-range communication pathways. Functionally important regions, including the L1 and L7/12 stalks, exhibit distinct, ion-dependent responses, while the L10–L11 region shows enhanced long-range coupling under varying ionic conditions. These results demonstrate that ionic composition modulates both local stability and global ribosomal dynamics, with implications for translational efficiency and fidelity.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: A hybrid mixture approach for clustering and characterizing biomedical data
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Kazeem A. Kareem, Fan Dai Model-based clustering (MBC) is widely used for identifying latent groups and characterizing heterogeneous structures in biomedical data. However, modern biomedical studies often generate datasets with large sample sizes and many variables, for which standard MBC approaches can be difficult to fit reliably and efficiently. Mixture of factor analyzers (MFA) addresses part of this challenge by representing high-dimensional covariance structures through a few underlying factors, thereby reducing the covariance dimensionality. However, current estimation methods for MFA are often computationally impractical for massive data due to the slow convergence of nested EM-type algorithms. Moreover, many existing implementations require a common number of latent factors across clusters, limiting their ability to capture group-specific structures. We propose a hybrid matrix-free computational scheme for accurate and efficient estimation of Gaussian mixture of factor analyzers, which avoids explicit construction or storage of large covariance matrices. We further develop a generalized version that allows different clusters to have varying numbers of factors, providing additional flexibility for group-specific characterization. Simulation studies show that the proposed approach achieves substantially faster convergence than the existing method, especially in high-dimensional settings, while preserving high clustering and estimation accuracy. Applications to the Wisconsin breast cancer dataset, a lymphoma gene-expression dataset, and a human brain single-cell RNA sequencing dataset demonstrate accurate identification of benign/malignant breast tumors, lymphoma subtypes, and neuronal and astrocytic cell populations. The fitted factor-loading structures reveal biologically meaningful differences in nuclear morphology for breast tumors, with malignant samples showing stronger irregularity-related variation, group-specific gene-expression heterogeneity among the three lymphoma subtypes, and distinct patterns of transcriptional variation between neurons and astrocytes, with neuronal variation reflecting a broader set of coordinated transcriptional directions and astrocytic variation concentrated in a more compact latent structure.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: Inferring population-level physiologically based model parameters for sleep in infancy and young childhood
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Lachlan Webb, Andrew J. K. Phillips, James A. Roberts The sleep patterns of infants and young children differ from adult sleep patterns, with longer duration and multiple bouts per 24 hours. There is also considerable heterogeneity in infant sleep, both between individuals and within individuals across development. While mathematical models have been used to understand the mechanisms that regulate adult sleep, the development of sleep from infancy through early childhood has remained largely unexplored. Here we used an established mathematical model for adult sleep regulation to investigate how the underlying mechanisms of sleep mature from ages 1 month to 5 years, and identify a basis for inter-individual differences at each age. Using a Bayesian approach to estimate joint distributions of model parameters at different ages, we found that: (i) decreases in the rate of accumulation of sleep homeostatic pressure captured the reduction in sleep duration across development; while (ii) increases in the time scale of the sleep homeostatic drive captured the consolidation of sleep into fewer sleep bouts per day across development. In terms of inter-individual differences, we found larger spread in the parameters within the earlier stages of infancy (24-h) cycles. These results establish plausible, population-level trajectories in physiological parameters underpinning maturation of sleep regulation through infancy and early childhood.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: Rollout models of human planning with exact action probabilities
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Jeroen Olieslagers, Wei Ji Ma One proposed mechanism for human planning is the mental simulation, or “rollout,” of potential action sequences to evaluate future outcomes. While rollout-based models have seen great success in artificial intelligence, cognitive models that describe how people use rollouts remain scarce, in part because they are difficult to fit to behavioral data. Existing methods rely on computationally intensive simulations that result in approximate, noisy estimates of latent planning parameters. We introduce ROSETTE (Rollouts with Stochastic Early Termination and Tractable Estimation), a rollout-based model for finite goal-directed tasks with absorbing goals that provides analytically tractable, simulation-free model fitting. ROSETTE treats planning as a sequence of mental simulations formalized as an absorbing Markov chain. The model deterministically accumulates analytically computed expected rollout evidence and performs a variable number of policy-update cycles. We fit ROSETTE to data from human participants in two multi-step planning tasks and found that it well accounted for a rich set of summary statistics of behavior. By making this specific class of absorbing-goal rollout models tractable, our framework provides a testable account of how people may simulate and evaluate possible futures.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: Simulation-guided design of exotendons to reduce the energetic cost of running
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Jon Stingel, Nicholas Bianco, Carmichael Ong, Steve Collins, Scott Delp, Jennifer Hicks A passive device that attaches to the feet, called an exotendon, can reduce the energetic cost of running at moderate speeds, but its efficacy and optimal design parameters at higher speeds are unknown. Identifying optimal parameters at new speeds experimentally would require many experimental trials with different exotendon designs, which is challenging for participants at higher running speeds. We developed a muscle-driven simulation framework to predict the effect of various exotendon designs on the energetic cost of running at an experimentally untested speed (4 m/s). We used these predictions to select four designs, which we evaluated experimentally as users ran at this speed. The framework correctly predicted that an exotendon that reduced energetic cost at 2.7 m/s would also reduce energetic cost at 4 m/s (10% predicted vs. 5.7% measured) and that a short, stiff exotendon and a long, compliant exotendon would not significantly reduce energetic cost. However, exotendon parameters predicted by the simulation to maximize energetic savings did not significantly reduce energetic cost when evaluated experimentally. There was variability between participants in both the magnitude of maximum energy savings and the exotendon condition associated with those savings. In a 5-km time trial performed with and without the exotendon condition that elicited the largest energy savings for each participant during the experiment, we observed a lower average heart rate (-3.9 ± 3.8 beats/min; P = 0.03; mean ± standard deviation) and increased cadence (15.9 ± 9.6 steps/min; P = 0.002) when participants ran with the exotendon but did not observe a statistically significant difference in finishing time (-13.5 ± 24.6 sec; P = 0.3). These results demonstrate exotendons can reduce energetic cost across multiple running speeds and that predictive simulations provide a framework for guiding experiments to evaluate assistive device designs.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: Pupil dynamics reflect uncertainty-driven adjustments of probability learning
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Aaron Greenhouse-Tucknott, Cedric Foucault, Anne Buot, Florent Meyniel Adaptive learning in dynamic environments depends on the brain’s ability to represent and respond to uncertainty. Changes in arousal-mediated pupil diameter provide insight into the neural basis of this process. Prior work has focused on magnitude-based inference tasks and revealed that learning is primarily influenced by the detection of change points and the corresponding modulation of arousal. In comparison, the role of arousal systems in learning contexts where changes are harder to detect, such as in probability learning, remains poorly understood. Here, we combined pupillometry with a probability learning task in which human participants estimated a hidden generative probability of stimuli that changed abruptly and unpredictably. A Bayesian ideal observer model was used to estimate trial-by-trial learning rates and two uncertainty-associated factors: change point probability (the probability that the generative process has abruptly changed) and prior uncertainty (about the current beliefs on this generative process). In line with normative theory, participants relied on prior uncertainty to adjust learning rates. Pupil analyses revealed temporally distinct representations of uncertainty, with phasic dilations tracking change point probability and tonic pupil dilations tracking prior uncertainty. Mediation analyses further indicated that both phasic and tonic pupil signals partially carried the effects of change point probability and prior uncertainty on learning, respectively. Critically, high tonic arousal weakened the coupling between phasic pupil responses and change point probability, accompanied by a reduced influence of change point probability on learning. Together, our results demonstrate that probability learning in a dynamic environment is underpinned by computationally rational integration of latent uncertainty factors and its contribution to belief updating,regulated through arousal-associated responses.

Water Research.title: Carbon availability and stability modulate chemoautotrophic carbon fixation in estuarine and coastal wetlands.
Water Research.abstract: Chemoautotrophic carbon fixation (CCF) is a critical pathway for microbial CO2 fixation; however, how carbon dynamics mediate the CCF process remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the influences of carbon availability, source, and stability on the CCF process in estuarine and coastal wetlands. CCF rates varied >20-fold, ranging from 7.6 to 177 ng C g-1 d-1 and decreasing with increasing organic carbon concentration. Autochthonous, marine, and terrestrial sources contributed 14.0-40.1%, 22.1-51.9%, and 22.1-60.0% of total organic carbon, respectively. Autochthonous carbon significantly correlated with iron-bound organic carbon (Fe-OC) concentration and CCF rate, suggesting that autochthonous carbon was crucial for Fe-OC formation and the chemoautotrophic process. The observed isotopic depletion of δ13C-SOC exhibited substantial consumption of labile organic carbon by anaerobic respiration, which was accompanied by the enhanced CCF rates. The isotopic enrichment of δ13C-Fe-OC and significant loss of Fe-OC indicated Fe-OC decoupling during anaerobic incubation. In addition, the relationship between CCF and carbon fraction was strongly influenced by the contrasting wetland habitats. Collectively, carbon availability and biogeochemical conditions jointly mediate chemoautotrophic activity, exerting a significant influence on allocation tradeoff and preferential preservation of organic carbon in estuarine and coastal wetlands.

Water Research.title: Enzyme-assisted bromination enables deep mineralization of trace urea by activating the rate-limiting intermediate.
Water Research.abstract: Bromination is practically applied for removing trace urea (μg·L-1) to meet the stringent requirements of electronic-grade ultrapure water, but it remains limited by slow kinetics at circumneutral pH, with the origin of this kinetic limitation not well understood. Here, the pH dependence of urea mineralization kinetics and pathways was systematically evaluated, while an enzyme-assisted bromination strategy was developed to relieve this limitation. The pH dependence was found to arise from bromination intermediates. Bromine reacts rapidly with urea regardless of pH, but the resulting monobromourea (pKa = 11.29) is brominated 55-fold more slowly in its neutral form than in its deprotonated form. Thus, it accumulates and dictates the overall rate below pH 10. Then, bromine was coupled with urea oligomerase to activate the accumulating intermediate rather than the parent compound. The enzyme did not alter the mineralization pathway or reaction order, but suppressed monobromourea accumulation and increased the apparent mineralization rate constant by 5.7-fold at pH 7.0. Theoretical calculations revealed that coordination of monobromourea at the dinickel site of enzyme polarizes its NH bond, conferring deprotonation-like electronic character and lowering the bromination barrier from 4.35 to 3.44 kcal·mol-1. Combined with downstream reverse osmosis, this approach can more efficiently polish the total organic carbon required for electronic-grade ultrapure water, demonstrating that targeting rate-limiting intermediates with enzyme-assisted bromination offers a general route to intensifying halogenation-based mineralization.

Water Research.title: Mechanisms of accelerated aging of microplastics and DOM release under cyclic environments: Underestimated environmental effects from freeze-thaw cycles.
Water Research.abstract: Microplastics (MPs) pollution is intensified by environmental aging. However, most studies have focused on individual aging conditions (e.g., continuous light or freezing), with less attention to the effects of cyclic environmental stressors on aging of MPs. Therefore, studying the impact of cyclic conditions on aging of MPs is of great significance for accurately reflecting their ecological risk. In this study, polystyrene (PS) and polylactic acid (PLA) were selected to systematically elucidate their aging mechanisms under light-dark alternation and freeze-thaw cycles, as well as the composition and characteristics of dissolved organic matter (DOM) released during aging. The results showed that, compared to their corresponding continuous conditions, light-dark alternation and freeze-thaw cycles increased the aging rate of MPs by 0.12-0.68-fold and 0.12-0.92-fold, respectively, suggesting that studies conducted under single aging conditions may underestimate their environmental impacts. Furthermore, compared with light-dark alternation, freeze-thaw cycles generated more reactive sites on MPs, thereby promoting hydrolysis and accelerating the aging of PLA-MPs (increased 0.46-fold). Distinct mechanisms were identified for the two cyclic aging processes: light-dark alternation primarily relies on light-driven •OH radicals, whereas freeze-thaw cycles are governed mainly by mechanical stress and/or hydrolysis. Meanwhile, freeze-thaw cycles generated less aromatic, higher-H/C DOM molecules, which have been reported to exhibit relatively high lability and potentially stronger short-term environmental disturbances. These findings highlight freeze-thaw cycles as an important driver of MP aging and associated DOM transformation, particularly for biodegradable plastics.

Water Research.title: Hydrology-guided intelligent spatiotemporal reconstruction method for sparse water quality data in urban watersheds.
Water Research.abstract: Nature-Based Systems are a critical approach to water management in urban watersheds. Assessing the effectiveness of such sustainable water management schemes depends fundamentally on sufficient and reliable water quality data. However, existing sparse monitoring networks lack continuous and reliable observation records, failing to meet the data requirements for monitoring spatiotemporal variations in water quality. Moreover, most conventional reconstruction methods are purely data-driven and lack the integration of hydrological knowledge, which hampers their capability to handle sparse observations in urban watersheds. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes a deep learning-based spatiotemporal reconstruction framework for water-quality and hydrometeorological data. The framework first reconstructs missing hydrometeorological driving sequences. Subsequently, it leverages the reconstructed hydrological sequences to guide the reconstruction of water quality data, transforming sparse 4-hourly observations into complete hourly series. Finally, a probabilistic forecasting module is built upon the high-resolution reconstructed series, outputting Gaussian predictive means and standard deviations to quantify uncertainty and estimate the probability of exceeding water quality standards. The method is validated using field monitoring data from six stations in the Huaxi River watershed, Chongqing. Experimental results indicate that the reconstructed hourly water quality series outperform the original 4-hourly data in capturing pollutant concentration variability, with Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency improvements ranging from 0.18 to 0.57. These results demonstrate that the framework serves short-term probabilistic forecasting and early warning of water quality standard exceedances, providing timely data support for pollution risk management in urban watersheds. The code that supports the findings of this study is openly available in the HG-STGNN repository on GitHub at https://github.com/Indig0Cat/HG-STGNN.

Water Research.title: Membrane distillation for sustainable freshwater-heat co-generation from geothermal brine in cold regions.
Water Research.abstract: As cold regions face growing demands for freshwater and space heating, geothermal brines offer a unique dual-resource advantage by supplying both thermal energy and viable desalination feedwater. However, the existing exploitation of this resource relies primarily on separate heat exchangers and thermal desalination processes, which are limited by singular functionality, low efficiency and scaling susceptibility. To fully harness this renewable energy potential, we develop a geothermal-driven multistage air-gap membrane distillation (AGMD) system for simultaneous freshwater production and heat extraction. During the process, the geothermal brine undergoes phase changes (i.e., evaporation-condensation) to yield freshwater, while the vapor-released latent heat is recovered, thereby achieving the freshwater-heat co-generation. The feasibility is demonstrated through coupled experiments and simulations, and by balancing the trade-off between system performance and capital cost, we identify a 16-stage configuration as the optimal design. Validated real-world simulations across 15 northern provinces in China confirm the high operational stability and broad deployability of the proposed system. Economically, for community-scale heating (100000 kWh day-1), the cogeneration cost is reduced to $0.0036 kWh-1, which is generally more than 20% below local market heating prices. Ultimately, our work provides a practical pathway for integrating geothermal utilization, freshwater supply and space heating in community services.

Water Research.title: Triplet-state dissolved organic matter drives solar reduction photochemistry through sulfite activation.
Water Research.abstract: Sulfite (S(IV)) activation has emerged as a promising strategy for micropollutant abatement, yet whether naturally occurring dissolved organic matter (DOM) can efficiently activate S(IV) and which reactive species are responsible for micropollutant transformation remain unclear. Here, using imidacloprid (IMI) as a model micropollutant, we demonstrate a pronounced synergistic effect between DOM photosensitization and S(IV) activation, increasing the observed IMI degradation rate constant to 5.21 times that in the Solar-S(IV) process. Triplet-state DOM (3DOM*) was identified as the primary species responsible for S(IV) activation. Laser flash photolysis tests with model photosensitizers revealed fast reactions between triplet species and S(IV), with second-order quenching rate constants ranging from 4.80(± 0.30) × 107 M-1 s-1 to 1.85(± 0.40) × 109 M-1 s-1 at pH 7.0. S(IV) activation by 3DOM* proceeds predominantly through electron transfer, while proton-coupled electron transfer provides an additional pathway that accelerates bisulfite activation. The long-overlooked sulfite radical (SO3•-), rather than conventional oxidizing radicals, was identified as the dominant species governing IMI degradation via reduction and radical-addition reactions. Collectively, these findings redefine 3DOM* as a photoredox mediator initiating reductive sulfur photochemistry, thereby establishing a mechanistic foundation for sustainable, solar-driven advanced reduction processes applicable to both natural and engineered aquatic environments.

Water Research.title: Membrane-aerated biofilm reactors (MABRs) are enriched with filamentous fungi at high carbon concentrations.
Water Research.abstract: Membrane-aerated biofilm reactors (MABRs) are an energy-efficient wastewater treatment technology based on biofilms grown on gas-permeable membranes. As with most wastewater treatment technologies, MABR biofilms are typically dominated by bacteria. However, here we show that MABRs supplied with high organic carbon loadings can be dominated by filamentous fungi, leading to stiff biofilms. When fed with food processing wastewater at approximately 550 mg COD L⁻¹, filamentous fungi accounted for 85% of the biofilm, compared to 30% for co-diffusional controls. The MABR biofilms showed EPS matrices enriched in protein and extracellular DNA, and were stiffer than co-diffusional biofilms. When supplied with 550 mg COD L⁻¹ acetate in minimal medium, filamentous fungi accounted for 67% of the biofilm and were dominated by Geotrichum and Galactomyces. In contrast, MABRs supplied with 150 mg COD L⁻¹ acetate had only 4% filamentous fungi. These findings identify filamentous fungi as important and overlooked members of MABR biofilms, especially for high carbon loadings. A potential benefit is that fungi can degrade recalcitrant compounds not degraded by bacteria. However, the biofilm's greater mechanical strength may lead to excessive biofilm accumulation and may require special measures to promote detachment.

Water Research.title: Surfactants as dynamic regulators of contaminant transport: From interfacial processes to groundwater remediation outcomes.
Water Research.abstract: Surfactants enter subsurface environments through remediation, industrial releases, wastewater infiltration, biological production, and consumer products. Their effects on contaminant fate are commonly interpreted through micellar solubilization and reduction of fluid-fluid interfacial tension. Whether these processes improve recovery or increase spreading depends on contaminant-bearing phase mobility, hydraulic contact and capture. By partitioning among aqueous, solid, fluid-fluid, and particle-associated domains, surfactants alter wettability, capillary forces, surface charge, sorption, colloidal stability, and carrier mobility, thereby redistributing contaminant mass among transport states with different mobilities. Here we synthesize these processes across molecular, pore, column, and aquifer scales and propose a conceptual diagnostic framework termed Surfactant-Interface-Mobility (SIM). SIM links the local formulation state, dynamic interfacial response and area, contaminant-state redistribution, phase-specific mobility, and hydraulic accessibility. Four diagnostic transport categories-retention, aqueous transfer including solubilization, nonaqueous-phase liquid (NAPL) mobilization, and carrier-facilitated transport-can coexist and evolve. Under effective hydraulic capture, surfactant-induced transitions can increase contaminant recovery; inadequate contact can leave source mass untreated, while inadequate capture can allow redistribution, plume expansion or downstream exposure. SIM organizes the measurements needed to distinguish these outcomes. Its predictive capability and incremental value relative to established transport models require independent validation.

Water Research.title: A quaternary ammonium-modified colloidal activated carbon for effective and selective capture of PFOA in groundwater: Mechanisms of multi-synergistic adsorption interactions.
Water Research.abstract: Based on the unique properties of perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), we developed a carbon-based adsorbent strategy by tailoring pore structures and introducing synergistic electrostatic, hydrophobic, and Lewis acid sites, leading to the fabrication of quaternary ammonium-modified colloidal activated carbon (QA-CAC) for PFOA adsorption in groundwater. QA-CAC exhibited superior PFOA adsorption capacity compared to commercial CAC, achieving over 90% removal within 3 min. According to Freundlich isotherm fitting, the adsorption capacity (Kf) reached 102.62 (mg/g)(mg/L)-0.49. When competing pollutants of various types coexisted, QA-CAC exhibited selective adsorption toward PFOA. Density functional theory calculations demonstrated that PFOA possessed a distinct thermodynamic preference over competing contaminants, with the strongest adsorption affinity and an adsorption energy of -2.93 eV. Common groundwater constituents did not significantly interfere with the adsorption capacity for PFOA. An artificial groundwater system was also selected to evaluate the adsorption and desorption performance of QA-CAC toward PFOA. Under different water matrices and external contaminants, PFOA previously adsorbed onto QA-CAC exhibited an extremely low desorption risk. Furthermore, QA-CAC suspension maintained excellent stability even after 20 days, and exhibited significantly enhanced mobility in simulated column. This work provides guidance for the design of efficient carbon-based adsorbents for in situ remediation of PFOA-contaminated groundwater.

Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution.title: Gene tree discordance, saturation, and marker properties shape phylogenomic conflict in squamates.
Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution.abstract: Phylogenomic studies of the same clades using different markers and methods can support highly confident yet conflicting species trees, obscuring evolutionary relationships and complicating comparative analyses. We investigated biological, molecular, and methodological sources of phylogenomic discordance in squamates by analyzing four genome-scale datasets representing three major marker classes: protein-coding genes, anchored hybrid enrichment loci, and ultra-conserved elements. We applied standardized alignment, filtering, tree-building, concordance factor, saturation, and simulation-based analyses, focusing on historically contentious relationships near the root of Squamata and within Toxicofera. Marker classes differed strongly in alignment length, informativeness, missing data, taxonomic coverage, gene tree concordance, and sensitivity to species tree method. Protein-coding genes yielded the lowest gene tree-species tree discordance and closest fit to model-conditional simulation expectations but did not definitively resolve all deep squamate relationships. Substitutional saturation shifted support among alternative placements of Dibamidae, Gekkota, and toxicoferan lineages, indicating that gene tree error contributes to uncertainty at ancient nodes. Minor topology asymmetry at some branches suggests more complex phylogenomic discordance than expected under incomplete lineage sorting alone. We found a lack of support for anomaly zone conditions across most of the deepest contentious splits in the squamate phylogeny. Overall, our results show that phylogenomic conflict in squamates reflects interactions among marker properties, saturation, gene tree error, model fit, and species tree method, and that resolving difficult phylogenomic problems requires evaluating the composition and behavior of marker datasets.

eLife.title: Ramping-up hippocampal ripples and their neocortical coupling support human visual short-term memory
eLife.abstract: Emerging evidence suggests that the hippocampus contributes to visual short-term memory (VSTM). However, the neural mechanisms through which hippocampal activity supports the maintenance of VSTM representations remain largely unknown. Here, using intracranial EEG recordings from human participants performing a delayed match-to-sample task for naturalistic objects, we investigated the role of hippocampal ripple activity—brief high-frequency oscillations associated with memory replay—in VSTM maintenance and hippocampal-neocortical communication. We found that hippocampal ripple rates progressively ramped up during the maintenance period and supported successful VSTM. More critically, hippocampal ripples were temporally coupled with the ripples in the lateral temporal lobe (LTL), and these coupled ripples were associated with memory reactivation in the LTL. These findings provide direct evidence that hippocampal–neocortical interaction via coupled ripples supports VSTM, extending the role of hippocampal ripples from long-term consolidation to short-term mnemonic processes and offering new insights into the dynamic coding mechanisms of working memory.

eLife.title: Calibrated analysis framework for nanopore direct RNA sequencing uncovers cell-specific m⁶A proportions at conserved sites
eLife.abstract: Nanopore direct RNA sequencing (DRS) coupled with Dorado modification-aware base calling enables mapping of epitranscriptomic modifications including N6-methyladenosine (m6A) at the level of individual RNAs. However, the sensitivity, specificity, and reproducibility of this method remain unclear and have only recently begun to be addressed through systematic benchmarking studies. Here, we aimed to establish a best-practice workflow for DRS-based epitranscriptomic analyses. Specifically, we evaluated multiple Dorado versions and models using RNA isolated from primary cells and unmodified in vitro transcribed RNAs. We further utilized an m6A methyltransferase inhibitor as a specificity control. We established that stringent filtering is necessary to reduce the contribution of background and found that Dorado predictions captured an increasing proportion of GLORI sites detected at high m6A/A proportions. Further, by applying DRS to a human primary fibroblast and a HD10.6 neuron dataset, we detected differences in the predicted m6A/A proportions at conserved sites between these datasets. Our study thus presents the first systematic comparison of Dorado and GLORI from the same input RNA and expands characterization of the m6A epitranscriptome to fibroblasts and neurons.

eLife.title: Integrating distributed lag non-linear models and deep learning reveals meteorological drivers of influenza A and B positivity in a 6-year subtropical surveillance study
eLife.abstract: Subtropical influenza forecasting is complicated by non-linear meteorological dynamics and surveillance bias stemming from pandemic-era testing fluctuations. Existing approaches either characterize lagged environmental associations without forecasting capacity or apply deep learning without epidemiological interpretability. We analyzed multisite influenza surveillance data from Putian, southeastern China (2018–2023); test positivity was the primary outcome to mitigate testing-related bias. Distributed lag nonlinear models estimated type-specific associations between eight meteorological variables and positivity over a 15-day lag window. A Bayesian-optimized long short-term memory (LSTM) network incorporating meteorological, autoregressive, and socio-behavioral covariates was benchmarked against covariate-matched multivariate autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) models. For influenza A, the temperature-associated relative risk (RR) peaked at 15°C (3.01; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.03–8.78), and positivity was associated with narrow diurnal temperature ranges. Influenza B positivity was associated with colder conditions (8°C; RR = 26.12, 95% CI: 7.79–87.61), higher humidity (91%; RR = 1.52, 95% CI: 1.00–2.29), and lower solar radiation. The LSTM had lower mean absolute error for influenza A (0.009 vs 0.136 for ARIMA and 0.138 for XGBoost) and B (0.002 vs 0.049 and 0.070); symmetric mean absolute percentage error was 0.521 vs 1.212 and 1.081 for A and 0.484 vs 0.810 and 0.737 for B. Covariate ablation and Shapley additive explanations analyses suggested that historical positivity and testing-related variables contributed to forecast stability. External validation in Sanming provided preliminary evidence of regional portability. This framework combines interpretable meteorological associations with short-horizon forecasting under variable surveillance conditions.

A kinetic error filtering mechanism for enzyme-free copying of nucleic acid sequences
eLife.abstract: Accurate copying of nucleic acid sequences is essential for self-replicating systems. Modern cells achieve error ratios as low as 10−9 with sophisticated enzymes capable of kinetic proofreading. In contrast, experiments probing enzyme-free copying of RNA and DNA as potential prebiotic replication processes find error ratios on the order of 10%. Given this low intrinsic copying fidelity, plausible scenarios for the spontaneous emergence of molecular evolution require an accuracy-enhancing mechanism. Here, we study a 'kinetic error filtering' scenario that dramatically boosts the likelihood of producing exact copies of nucleic acid sequences. The mechanism exploits the observation that initial errors in template-directed polymerization of both DNA and RNA are likely to trigger a cascade of consecutive errors and significantly stall downstream extension. We incorporate these characteristics into a mathematical model with experimentally estimated parameters, and leverage this model to probe to what extent accurate and faulty polymerization products can be kinetically discriminated. Limiting the time window for polymerization prevents completion of erroneous strands, resulting in a pool in which full-length products show an enhanced accuracy. This comes at the price of a concomitant reduction in yield. However, the yield rate and the fidelity can be simultaneously increased by kinetic error filtering, if the templates are not too long. Within cyclically varying environments, e.g., temperature cycles in hydrothermal systems, repeated copying attempts could produce exact copies of sequences as long as 50mers within their lifetime, facilitating the emergence and maintenance of catalytically active oligonucleotides.

eLife.title: Blood-derived dietary protein promotes sleep in the mosquito Aedes aegypti
eLife.abstract: Sleep is a ubiquitous, yet highly variable, behavior across species. The duration and timing of sleep are influenced by ecological demands and dietary context. In the mosquito Aedes aegypti, a blood-feeding insect with specialized nutritional requirements, the relationship between feeding and sleep remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated how blood-derived dietary protein influences sleep regulation. Using postural analysis, videography, and arousal-threshold assays, we established that immobility bouts of ≥10 min reliably define sleep in A. aegypti. Mosquitoes lacking the circadian clock gene cycle still maintained daily sleep rhythms but exhibited reduced sleep duration and heightened overall activity. Infrared activity monitoring revealed that blood-fed females showed a marked increase in sleep beginning immediately after feeding and persisting for several days, accompanied by reduced locomotor activity. Notably, this sleep elevation lasted well beyond the cessation of previously reported host-seeking phases, raising the possibility of distinct phases of opportunistic vs. targeted host pursuit. To determine the dietary basis of this effect, we tested mosquitoes fed a bovine serum albumin (BSA)-based diet. BSA feeding alone was sufficient to mimic the sleep-promoting and activity-reducing effects of blood, suggesting dietary protein is a major nutritional regulator. Moreover, RNAi-mediated knockdown of the leucokinin receptor (Lkr), which has previously been associated with fluid homeostasis and feeding behavior, resulted in enhanced sleep and reduced activity, implicating mosquito LK signaling in the modulation of postprandial sleep. Together, these findings demonstrate that blood-derived proteins drive sustained increases in sleep and reductions in locomotor activity in A. aegypti. This work positions A. aegypti as a model for dissecting nutrient-specific regulation of sleep and highlights potential adaptive functions of protein-induced quiescence, such as energy conservation and predator avoidance. More broadly, it provides insight into how specialized diets shape the neural and behavioral architecture of sleep.

eLife.title: Cognitive control networks in human and macaque
eLife.abstract: A much-replicated finding in human brain imaging is a distributed ‘multiple-demand’ or MD system, increasing in activity for many kinds of cognitive demand, and centrally involved in cognitive control. MD regions are proposed to encode a distributed mental model of critical task events, bound together in the roles and relationships needed to direct action selection. Though previous data hint at a corresponding network in the macaque, there has been no direct comparison to human data. Here we used functional magnetic resonance imaging to measure whole-brain activation in a multi-step saccadic maze task, compared to a control requiring similar moves but without goal-based decisions. Human data were a close match to the canonical MD network, extended to include adjacent regions, and in particular much of the canonical dorsal attention network. Data from two monkeys suggested correspondences in dorsomedial frontal, insula/orbitofrontal, and posterior temporal cortex. Carbon monoxide utilization by Thermanaeromonas species and description of Thermobium azorense gen. nov., sp. nov.
FEMS Microbiology Ecology.abstract: Syngas fermentation by carbon monoxide (CO)-utilizing acetogens offers a sustainable route for converting gasified waste materials into value-added chemicals. In this study, we isolated a novel thermophilic CO-utilizing bacterium, strain AZ2, from marine hydrothermal sediment collected on the island of São Miguel, Azores, Portugal. Strain AZ2 is an obligately anaerobic, spore-forming bacterium. Average nucleotide identity (ANI) and digital DNA-DNA hybridization (dDDH) analyses indicate that strain AZ2 represents a novel species within a previously uncharacterized lineage represented by the GTDB placeholder genus UBA 12545 in Neomoorellaceae. It is also the first cultured representative of this genus. Strain AZ2 was able to consume CO, producing acetate. We further demonstrated that its closest isolated relatives-Thermanaeromonas toyohensis and Thermanaeromonas sp. strain 9S-are capable of utilizing CO, producing either acetate or hydrogen gas (H2). Additionally, we unveiled the genomic potential for CO utilization within other members of the GTDB placeholder class DSM-521 (previously Moorellia) to which our isolate belongs, expanding the list of possible thermophilic CO-utilizing acetogens. We propose that strain AZ2T represents the type strain of a novel genus and species, named Thermobium azorense gen. nov., sp. nov. (= DSM 121889T = JCM 39698T).

FEMS Microbiology Ecology.title: Host species identity drives temporally stable octocoral microbiomes in Florida.
FEMS Microbiology Ecology.abstract: Octocorals are foundational components of Caribbean reef ecosystems, yet their bacterial microbiomes remain poorly characterized compared to scleractinian corals. We present an extensive 16S rRNA gene survey of western Atlantic octocoral microbiomes, characterizing 180 samples from four co-occurring South Florida species over three years: the encrusting species Briareum asbestinum and Erythropodium caribaeorum, and the branching species Eunicea flexuosa and Muricea muricata. Host species identity was the strongest predictor of microbiome composition, explaining 14.4% of bacterial community variation, while temporal and spatial factors contributed <2% each. Core microbiome analysis at three prevalence thresholds (80%, 90%, and 100%) revealed host-specific bacterial associations. All four species harbored largely host-specific Endozoicomonas ASVs as dominant core members, with encrusting species maintaining larger and more taxonomically diverse cores than branching species. Phylogenetic reconstruction placed the dominant Endozoicomonas ASVs among described Endozoicomonas species, three lineages related to E. euniceicola, which was described from Florida octocorals, while the dominant Mycoplasma ASVs were highly divergent from described type strains, suggesting undescribed octocoral-associated lineages. Differential abundance analysis identified only a few significant temporally or spatially variable ASVs, reinforcing overall community stability. These findings demonstrate strong host control over microbial associations and provide a phylogenetic framework for understanding octocoral-bacteria symbioses in the western Atlantic.

FEMS Microbiology Ecology.title: The RNA virome of intertidal kelp in New Zealand reveals novel viral lineages associated with unhealthy kelp.
FEMS Microbiology Ecology.abstract: Pathogens can have major impacts on ecosystem function, especially when they infect foundational taxa such as habitat-forming kelp. Understanding which potentially pathogenic microbes are in an ecosystem is increasingly important as environmental change intensifies ecosystem imbalances, yet few studies have examined which viruses are associated with key habitat-forming macroalgae. Here, we screened multiple populations of intertidal / shallow-subtidal macroalgae in New Zealand for viruses. Samples were collected from three southern bull kelp species: Durvillaea antarctica, Durvillaea poha, and Durvillaea willana. Total RNA was extracted and sequenced from both obviously 'unhealthy' kelp tissue and apparently 'healthy' tissue. We identified putative novel viral lineages belonging to the families Mitoviridae, Narnaviridae, Partitiviridae, Totiviridae, and the recently proposed Ormycovirus group. Viral abundance and diversity were notably higher at Lawyers Head (the site closest to a city) compared to other sites, especially in unhealthy kelp samples. The elevated viral presence at Lawyers Head may indicate that human impacts, such as pollution, are influencing viral prevalence. This study reveals that coastal macroalgae in New Zealand host diverse viral lineages, some likely pathogenic, and hints at the potential influence of anthropogenic pollution on marine virome composition.

mSystems.title: Multi-omics characterization of different dietary fiber levels on microbiota and metabolism in Erhualian and large white pigs.
mSystems.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Erhualian pigs (EHL) exhibit tolerance to high-fiber diets, yet the underlying mechanisms involving gut microbiota and metabolism remain unclear. Here, we integrated colonic short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) profiling, 16S rRNA sequencing, and liver metabolomics to evaluate the effects of graded wheat bran fiber levels (total dietary fiber [TDF]: 14.07%, 16.32%, 17.99%, and 18.85%) on fiber digestibility, gut microbiota, and metabolism in EHL, compared with two large white pigs (LW) groups: large LW (LLW, same initial physiological stage as EHL) and small LW (SLW, same initial body weight as EHL). Apparent total tract digestibility (ATTD) of TDF in EHL was unaffected by increasing TDF intake (P > 0.05), whereas ATTD of TDF and insoluble dietary fiber in LLW decreased significantly (P < 0.01). High-fiber diet elevated acetate and butyrate, and total SCFAs in LLW (P < 0.05), but only trended toward higher isobutyrate and isovalerate in EHL (0.05 < P < 0.1). Regardless of diet, EHL exhibited higher colonic microbiota diversity (Simpson, P < 0.05) than LW, whereas richness (Chao and ACE) was unaffected by diet or breed (P > 0.05). Breed was the primary factor shaping swine gut microbiota (P < 0.05), with diet showing a trend toward significance, shaping colonic microbiota (P = 0.0586). Multi-omics integration identified 29 key genera and 10 metabolites associated with high-fiber digestibility in EHL. These key bacteria and metabolites were co-enriched in carbohydrate metabolism pathways, including butanoate metabolism and starch and sucrose metabolism, and collectively contribute to the high-fiber digestibility phenotype. [IMPORTANCE] Indigenous Chinese pig breeds, such as the Erhualian pig (EHL), exhibit a superior capacity for high-fiber tolerance compared with commercial lean-type breeds, which currently account for approximately 90% of China's pig inventory. Reliance on lean-type breeds has increased concentrate feed demand, intensifying human-livestock food competition. While low-cost unconventional feedstuffs (such as rice bran and wheat bran) are available, their high insoluble fiber content limits utilization in modern breeds. Elucidating the mechanisms underlying the high-fiber tolerance of EHL is of critical importance, specifically the gut microbiota, metabolites that enable efficient utilization of higher fiber levels. In this study, we integrated colonic short-chain fatty acid (SCFA), microbiome profiling, liver metabolomics, and functional correlation analyses to demonstrate that the high-fiber digestibility of EHL is associated with breed-specific microbial compositional features and a distinct hepatic metabolic profile, characterized by enrichment of carbohydrate and butanoate metabolism. The integration of microbiota functional prediction and metabolomic data reveals potential microbial-host co-metabolic networks that underpin this phenotype. Collectively, this work will advance understanding of the metabolic and microbial mechanisms underlying high-fiber tolerance, offering potential strategies for improving feed efficiency in monogastric animals through microbiome and metabolic modulation.

mSystems.title: The ecological impact of Ulva prolifera green tide outbreaks: microbial connectivity and metabolic divergence.
mSystems.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Green tides in coastal areas have become an increasing eco-environmental concern around the world. However, the influence of massive green tides on microorganism dispersal has not yet been explored in detail. In this study, we used amplicon and metagenomic sequencing to first systematically examine the dynamics of the microbial community among continuous microhabitats in the Ulva prolifera bloom area. We found that the phycospheric microbiota exhibited increased α-diversity and complex network topologies. The tracking of bacterial sources indicated that phycospheric microorganisms originated from the algal-surface microhabitat and were widely shared with the surrounding seawater, indicating that U. prolifera blooms strengthen horizontal connectivity among microhabitats and thus facilitate the dispersal of phycospheric microorganisms into the surrounding seawater. With respect to microbial assemblages, the phycosphere was governed primarily by deterministic processes, indicating that environmental factors strongly influence the community structure of the phycosphere. Furthermore, genes involved in carbon degradation, nitrogen retention, and sulfate reduction were enriched in the algal surfaces and phycosphere, facilitating the transformation and accumulation of complex algae-derived organic matter into dissolved organic matter. Bacteroidia, Gammaproteobacteria, and Alphaproteobacteria were the key taxa contributing to organic matter transformation in the phycosphere and algal surfaces, likely reflecting their high substrate utilization strategies. In general, these findings highlight the microscale dynamics and ecological risks of microbial dispersal and demonstrate the combined effects of large-scale U. prolifera blooms on microbial structure and function, thus forming a precise assessment of the effects of macroalgal blooms on marine biogeochemical cycles. [IMPORTANCE] Ulva prolifera green tides are among the largest macroalgal blooms worldwide, yet how these events reshape microbial communities and their ecological functions remains poorly understood. This study reveals that green tide formation restructures microbial connectivity across algal-associated habitats and promotes distinct microbial metabolic strategies involved in organic matter transformation. These findings improve our understanding of how large-scale macroalgal blooms alter coastal microbial processes and provide new insights into the ecological consequences of expanding green tide events.

Lancet Microbe.title: Antimicrobial prescribing and guideline adherence in febrile inpatients in the Masanga Fever Study (MaFeStu) in Sierra Leone: a substudy within a prospective observational study.
Lancet Microbe.abstract: [BACKGROUND] Antimicrobial resistance is increasing in sub-Saharan Africa, yet detailed data on prescribing practices remain scarce. We aimed to characterise antimicrobial compounds prescribed at admission, assess their concordance with treatment guidelines, and examine antimicrobial compounds prescribed during hospitalisation. [METHODS] We conducted a substudy of the Masanga Fever Study (MaFeStu), a prospective observational study of febrile inpatients at Masanga Teaching Hospital in rural Sierra Leone from Sept 26, 2023, to Sept 26, 2024. Patients aged 5 months or older who were assessed within 3 h of admission and had documented fever (tympanic temperature >37·5°C) or reported fever within the previous 72 h were eligible. Patients were excluded if study procedures would delay urgent care, and those without available medication records were excluded post hoc. Clinical data and diagnoses were recorded prospectively, and antimicrobial prescriptions were extracted from patient files after discharge. The primary outcome was concordance of antimicrobial compounds initiated at admission with the hospital protocol and WHO guidance, assessed using predefined decision rules. Prescribed compounds were also classified by WHO Access, Watch, and Reserve category and indication. Secondary analyses summarised antimicrobial compounds prescribed during hospitalisation, including oral step-down and culture-directed therapy. [FINDINGS] 689 febrile inpatients included in the analysis, the median age was 14 years (IQR 1·8-34·0), 358 (52%) were female, and race and ethnicity data were not collected. At admission, 487 (71%; 95% CI 67-74) patients received one or more antimicrobial compounds. Of 882 antimicrobial compounds prescribed, 573 (65%; 95% CI 62-68) were WHO Access antibiotics, and 309 (35%; 95% CI 32-38) were WHO Watch antibiotics. Ceftriaxone was the most frequently prescribed compound (268 [30%] of 882). Lower respiratory tract infections, sepsis, and skin and soft tissue infections accounted for the largest share of compounds prescribed, overall and within the Watch category. Overall, 650 (74%; 95% CI 71-77) of 882 prescribed compounds were concordant with the hospital protocol, compared with 491 (56%; 95% CI 52-59) under WHO guidance. Discordant prescribing under both guidelines was concentrated in common indications, particularly sepsis and lower respiratory tract infection. During hospitalisation, 58 (4·9%; 95% CI 3·8-6·3) of 1183 antimicrobial compounds prescribed represented oral step-down therapy, and 73 (6·2%; 95% CI 4·9-7·7) were culture-directed. [INTERPRETATION] Most prescribed compounds were WHO Access antibiotics and were largely concordant with hospital guidance and, to a lesser extent, with WHO guidance. Prescribing patterns suggest that strengthening diagnostics, refining treatment guidelines, and improving guideline familiarity could enhance guideline-concordant prescribing and antimicrobial stewardship in similar settings with constrained diagnostic and stewardship resources.
